meta.title: What it costs a GB supplier to win a customer, and to keep one
meta.subtitle: Acquisition is a commission you pay someone else. Retention is margin you give up yourself. They are different kinds of thing, and since 2022 the law says so.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here is from a published source — Ofgem licence conditions, the CMA Energy Market Investigation, or a cited industry rate. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page, and no number on this page was chosen because a number was needed.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem SLC 22B (Ban on Acquisition-only Tariffs) and its Market-wide Derogation, consultation of 27 August 2025; CMA Energy Market Investigation 2016, Appendix 9.10 paragraphs 64 and 74; Ofgem price cap EBIT methodology consultation May 2023, paragraphs 4.24-4.25; PCW commission rates as cited in docs/market_research/B2_CATEGORY6_CAC_ANCHORS.md
claim_freshness.note: Written because the simulation carried four invented acquisition and retention constants with no source, while sourced research answering the same questions already existed in the repository and reached no code. The page exists so that the next invented number has something to contradict it.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Winning a domestic customer costs a GB supplier a commission paid to whoever introduced them — around £25 to £30 per fuel through a comparison site — while keeping one costs margin the supplier gives up in the price it charges, not cash it pays out; and since April 2022 a licence condition has made the second the only lawful way to offer a better deal to someone who is already yours.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
There are two quite different money flows and it is easy to model them as one. ACQUISITION is money leaving the business: a comparison site or a broker introduces a customer and invoices for it. You can point at the payment. RETENTION is money never arriving: you offer the customer a lower price than they would otherwise have paid, they stay, and the gap shows up as revenue you did not earn. Nobody sends an invoice for a retention offer.

The distinction is not bookkeeping pedantry. A cash cost and a foregone margin behave differently in every direction that matters: one hits the P&L at signup and the other bleeds across the whole term; one is the same whatever the customer consumes and the other scales with their volume; one weakens the balance sheet immediately and the other never appears on it at all. A model that charges a flat cash sum for a retention offer will get the timing, the size and the balance-sheet consequence all wrong at once, and each error will look small on its own.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
ACQUISITION. The CMA set out what the cost is made of: 'Customer acquisition costs comprise doorstep/energy advisers' costs, telesales, commissions payable to brokers or PCWs, sales support, proposition development and other similar costs' (Energy Market Investigation 2016, Appendix 9.10 paragraph 64). The same paragraph records that both UK GAAP and IFRS require firms to expense those costs as incurred, so a customer relationship a supplier built itself never appears on its balance sheet — only one it bought from someone else does.

That accounting treatment is not how the economics work, and the CMA said so. For its return-on-capital analysis it amortised acquisition costs over the average customer lifespan reported by the six large suppliers: those 'varied significantly (from around four to ten years), but with a concentration of values around six years', and the CMA used six years as its base case and eight as a sensitivity (paragraph 74). Ofgem later adopted the same six-year figure in the price cap's EBIT methodology, describing it as 'in line with the CMA's approach to amortising customer acquisition costs'.

RETENTION. Since April 2022 this has been a matter of licence law rather than commercial preference. Standard Licence Condition 22B, the Ban on Acquisition-only Tariffs, stops a supplier offering a fixed-term deal to new customers that it does not also offer its existing ones. Introduced alongside the Market Stabilisation Charge as a temporary response to wholesale volatility, the MSC ended on 31 March 2024 and the BAT was kept, extended annually; Ofgem's consultation of 27 August 2025 proposes extending it to 31 March 2027.

What makes retention possible under that ban is a specific carve-out. In Ofgem's own words, 'The BAT's Market-wide Derogation, which was introduced at the same time as the BAT, enables suppliers to offer bespoke, retention-only deals to their existing customers when they are coming to the end of a fixed-term deal.' A retention offer is therefore a TARIFF — a price, offered at a defined moment in the customer's contract — and the derogation exists precisely because it is a price rather than a payment.

CHANNELS. Comparison sites are the largest single route to a domestic customer and they are paid per switch, at a rate independent of what the customer goes on to consume. Business customers mostly arrive through brokers, and brokers are not paid that way at all: the commission is an ongoing per-unit adder embedded in the customer's own unit rate for the life of the contract, typically 0.5 to 2.0 pence per kWh for a small business and less for larger sites. A broker-introduced customer therefore costs more the more they use, and costs nothing at signup.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A supplier's acquisition spend should be lumpy and front-loaded against a customer book that pays back slowly: cash out at signup, margin in over something like six years. Growth should therefore look expensive in the year it happens and cheap in retrospect, which is exactly why the CMA amortised it.

The cost per domestic customer acquired through a comparison site should sit in tens of pounds, not hundreds — around £25 to £30 per fuel, so roughly £50 to £60 for a dual-fuel household. A figure in the low hundreds would imply a channel other than a comparison site, most likely direct brand marketing, for which no GB-energy-specific published benchmark appears to exist.

Business acquisition should not appear as a one-off cost line at all. It should appear as a per-kWh deduction running the length of the contract, which means a large business customer costs far more to have acquired than a small one, and the cost keeps arriving after the sale.

A retention offer should appear as reduced revenue on the retained account, concentrated at the renewal point and persisting for the term — never as a cost line. Two suppliers charging the same headline rate, one of which retained half its book with 5% discounts, should differ in revenue and not in operating costs.

And acquisition spend should show up in the balance sheet, not just the P&L. The CMA recorded the mechanism plainly: 'by growing rapidly a firm incurred significant customer acquisition costs up-front, which it expected to recover over the lifetime of the customers. However, such costs weakened a firm's balance sheet ... increasing the perceived riskiness of the supplier and, therefore, the quantity of collateral that trading counterparties required from the firm.'

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
The published anchors this page rests on, with what each one does and does not support.

WHAT IS SOURCED. The composition of acquisition cost and its accounting treatment (CMA Appendix 9.10 §64). The six-year amortisation base case, drawn from a reported spread of four to ten years (§74), and Ofgem's later adoption of the same figure. The existence, start date and current extent of SLC 22B, and the Market-wide Derogation that permits retention-only deals at end of fixed term. Comparison-site commission of roughly £25 to £30 per fuel switched. Broker commission bands of 0.2 to 2.0 pence per kWh by size band.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWABLE FROM THE PUBLIC RECORD. The actual per-customer acquisition costs the six large suppliers reported to the CMA are redacted in the published appendix. Every per-customer figure in that section that would settle the question is shown as an empty bracket. A supplier-specific GB acquisition cost is therefore not available at all, and any single number presented as one is an estimate wearing a citation.

ONE NEAR MISS, RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS THE FAILURE THIS PAGE EXISTS TO PREVENT. A search summary offered '£90 per customer' as an Ofgem acquisition-cost benchmark. Reading the source shows paragraph 4.24 is calculating depreciation and amortisation of FIXED ASSETS, and the £90 is that; what paragraph 4.25 shares with the CMA is only the six-year lifetime. Publishing £90 as an acquisition benchmark would have produced an invented number with a real citation attached, which is worse than an invented number, because the citation stops anyone checking.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
No GB-energy-specific figure for direct or brand-marketing acquisition could be found in any public source searched. A cross-industry cost-per-lead multiplied by an assumed conversion rate gives something in the low hundreds of pounds per customer, but that is two estimates stacked on each other and should not be treated as an anchor.

No published source breaks acquisition cost out at the residential/SME boundary. Small businesses plausibly arrive through both comparison-style and broker channels, and the split between them is not published.

The comparison-site rate is cited from secondary commentary on a CMA-era figure rather than from a rate card, and no supplier publishes what it actually pays. Commission rates are commercially negotiated and are very unlikely to be uniform.

The practical effect of the BAT on what suppliers actually offer at renewal is not quantified here. The derogation permits retention deals; how deep they are, and whether they cluster at particular discount levels, is not something the licence condition tells us.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not establish a single number to use for acquisition cost, and that is deliberate. The honest output of this research is a SHAPE — a per-switch commission for domestic, a per-kWh trail for business, a foregone margin for retention, and a six-year horizon over which any of it pays back — together with an explicit statement that the per-customer magnitude the six large suppliers actually reported is redacted from the public record.

It does not establish what our own supplier should spend. That is a company decision the simulation should be free to get wrong, not a constant to be calibrated until the answer looks right.

It does not cover customer-service cost to serve, bad debt, or the cost of losing a customer, all of which sit in the same P&L neighbourhood and none of which this page researched.

And it does not, by itself, change any code. What it does is make a specific class of future mistake visible: any acquisition or retention figure that appears in this repository without a source can now be held against a page that says what the published evidence actually supports, and what it does not.

meta.title: How a GB household chooses an energy deal, and why most of them don't
meta.subtitle: Almost nobody deliberately chooses a standard variable tariff, and most of the country is on one. Both of those are true at once, and the reason is that choosing and paying are separated by years.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB household almost never chooses a standard variable tariff and yet most households are on one, because a standard variable tariff is what you get when you do nothing — so the majority state of the market is the outcome of an absence of decisions rather than the sum of them, and the small minority who do act each year act overwhelmingly on price.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
There are two populations and they are easy to confuse because they are described with the same words.

The FLOW is the households who did something this year: compared, switched, renewed onto a new fixed deal. They are a minority, they are mostly acting on price, and almost all of them end up on a fixed-term contract, because that is what is on offer when you go looking.

The STOCK is everybody, and the stock is majority standard variable. Not because those households weighed a variable tariff against a fixed one and preferred the variable one — hardly anybody does that — but because a standard variable tariff is the default: it is where you land if you never engaged, where you roll to if your fixed deal ended and you did not act, and what you are put on if you move into a property and inherit the incumbent supplier.

So the two statements "almost everyone who switches takes a fixed deal" and "most households are on a variable deal" are both true, and a model that draws a household's tariff type from the stock share is modelling the wrong thing. The stock share is an OUTCOME of a behaviour, not an input to it.

The practical consequence for anyone modelling this: engagement and price sensitivity are different quantities and must stay separate. A household that has never switched at any price is disengaged, not price-insensitive. It can become extremely responsive the moment a bill shock makes it look.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
WHAT A HOUSEHOLD WEIGHS. Ofgem's consumer research (BMG fieldwork, n=3,235) puts price importance at between 35% and 44% across every subgroup it reports — a spread of about 1.26 times between the least and most price-focused groups. That is a striking result and it points the opposite way from intuition: GB households weight price fairly HOMOGENEOUSLY. Customer service sits second at around 32%, and the largest published spread between subgroups anywhere in that research is satisfaction-driven, at about 1.46 times — larger than price's. Exit fees account for around 22% of the switching decision overall, and 17% of respondents disproportionately prioritise exit fees over other factors: a published minority operating a genuinely different decision rule.

WHY THEY LEAVE, WHEN THEY LEAVE. Ofgem asked households who had switched in the previous six months why they had compared or switched (Consumer Impacts of Market Conditions survey, fieldwork January–February 2024, base 174 switchers, multi-code). The answers: get a cheaper tariff 44%; the supplier has a good reputation 19%; issues with the current supplier or tariff 16%; my supplier's customer service is poor, so I want to move 16%; the supplier offers good customer service 15%.

Business customers answer a different question with a different shape. Ofgem's non-domestic research (fieldwork July–September 2024, base 365 switchers) found the leading prompts were: knew the contract was coming to an end 29%; a price-increase notification from the previous supplier 16%; wanted a better deal 14%; a renewal notice from the existing supplier 12%; offered a better deal from a new supplier 9%. Around a third of businesses (33%) changed contract in the past twelve months, and service quality does not appear in the top five at all.

The two lists differ in kind and not only in ranking. The domestic list is dominated by a PRICE MOTIVE. The business list is dominated by a CONTRACTUAL EVENT — the top and fourth answers together describe the end of a term arriving and being noticed. That is a real structural difference: business contracts end and someone whose job it is notices, and domestic ones end and mostly nobody does.

HOW OFTEN ANYONE DOES ANYTHING. Switching collapsed during the crisis and is recovering: Ofgem's own summary is that switching rates are "gradually recovering from the post-crisis trough in 2021/2022, when almost all tariffs were set at the price cap", and remain below pre-crisis levels. Intent runs ahead of action and is itself low and falling: 21% said they were likely to switch in the next three months in January–February 2024, down nine points since July 2023.

WHAT MAKES SWITCHING WORTH DOING AT ALL. The re-emergence of fixed-term contracts after the crisis is what restored the reason to look. Ofgem records that the share of domestic customers on fixed-term contracts "more than doubled, rising from 11% to 27%" over the second half of 2023, and that as of February 2025 the differential between the cheapest tariffs and the price cap was around £140 a year. During 2022 that differential ran the other way: fixed deals were available and priced far above the cap, because a supplier pricing a year of hedged risk had to sit above a cap set on a backward-looking observation window. Households declined them and were, in the event, mostly wrong to.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A book's tariff mix should be a RESULT. If you model engagement, term ends and home moves, the fixed/variable split should fall out of them and should land in the published range — a domestic fixed share that is a minority in every year of 2016–2025, roughly 10% to 46%, centred near a third. If you have to set the split directly to hit that range, you have modelled the symptom.

Departures should be bimodal in time, not uniform. A fixed-term book should show a spike of decisions at term ends and near-silence between them; a variable book should show a low, steady trickle with no term structure at all and occasional storms when a cap change or a bill lands. A world where departures arrive at a constant hazard is a world with no contracts in it.

The response to price should be in POUNDS and not in percent. Ofgem's finding is that consumers value savings in absolute terms rather than in proportion to their bill, so a large house and a small flat facing the same percentage saving are not facing the same decision, and the large house should respond more.

Crisis years should look like a PRICE effect and not a scarcity effect. Fixed deals existed in 2022; they were expensive. A model that removes the fixed product in 2022 reproduces the right switching numbers through the wrong mechanism, and will then get the recovery wrong, because what recovered was the spread and not the availability.

And the reason distribution should not be flat. Somewhere near half of domestic departures should be price-motivated and a substantial minority service-motivated, with the service share invisible to anyone looking only at prices.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED, with its base. The domestic switching-motivation distribution (Ofgem CIM survey, January–February 2024, base 174). The business switching-prompt distribution and the 33% annual contract-change rate (Ofgem non-domestic 2024 research, July–September 2024, base 1,000, switcher base 365). Switching intent at 21% for the next three months, down nine points since July 2023 (CIM wave 5, n=3,439). The fixed-term share rising 11% to 27% over the second half of 2023, and a cheapest-versus-cap differential of about £140 in February 2025 (Ofgem State of the Market, April 2025). Price importance of 35–44% across subgroups, service at 32%, exit fees at 22% with a 17% minority prioritising them (Ofgem/BMG, n=3,235). The domestic fixed/variable stock split by year (already held at docs/market_research/svt_rates_active_passive_2016_2025.md, H confidence).

TWO CAUTIONS ABOUT THE MOTIVATION FIGURES, because they are the most quotable numbers here and the easiest to misuse. First, the base is 174 people and the question is multi-code, so the percentages do not sum to 100 and none of them carries a tight interval. Second and more important, it is a STATED reason from people who had ALREADY SWITCHED. It is not a hazard, it does not tell you the rate at which any cause produces a departure, and it cannot tell you anything at all about the households who did not move. Using it as a set of cause weights requires saying so.

A THIRD CAUTION, ABOUT SWITCHING VOLUMES, AND THE SERIES IT NO LONGER REFUSES (updated 2026-08-30). Published switching counts in this area are not one series. Some count electricity meter-point transfers, some count gas, some count changes of supplier across both fuels, and some count customers who switched supplier OR tariff. A figure of a few million for one year and a figure of a few million for another can be two different quantities, and dividing one by the other produces a number that is not a rate of anything. The rule that follows is the one this area keeps breaking: a both-fuel numerator divided by an electricity account base double-counts every dual-fuel household and reads roughly 1.8 times high.

This page previously declined to publish a year-by-year series for that reason. It now publishes ONE, on a stated pair, because the pair could be settled: EXTERNAL changes of supplier on a GB domestic ELECTRICITY meter point, over ALL GB domestic electricity accounts — including the households half way through a fixed term who are in the denominator and cannot be in the numerator. On that pair: 2016 17.0–17.6%, 2017 13.5–14.0%, 2018 19.5–20.0%, 2019 20.7–21.3%, 2020 22.5–23.0%, 2021 17.9–18.4%, 2022 2.9–4.3%, 2023 8.9–12.5%, 2024 12.5–16.1%, 2025 14.3–17.9%. Sources: DESNZ Quarterly Domestic Energy Switching Statistics and Energy UK switching statistics, corroborated live at 2020 and 2021 against Energy UK and GOV.UK. Each figure is a switch count over a ~28m account base, so it is a BAND and not a point.

What is still refused, and why. ElectraLink's headline series (3.21m changes of supplier in 2024, a stated peak of 6.34m in 2019) is NOT folded into those bands, because this pass could not settle whether it counts one fuel or two. Read as electricity its 2024 is 11.5%; read as both fuels the electricity share is about 1.8m and its 2024 is about 6.5%. Those differ by 1.8 times, and choosing between them to widen a band would be picking a number because a number was needed. It is recorded beside the series as an open question with what would settle it: Ofgem's Retail Market Indicators publish the switching series split by fuel, and its April 2026 reading — 243,754 electricity and 183,180 gas domestic switches in one month — would settle both the definition and the recent level if taken from the table rather than read off the chart.

AND ONE THING THIS RATE IS NOT. It is not an upper bound on a supplier's own losses, which is how it is easy to read it. Total switches equal the sum of suppliers' external losses and total accounts equal the sum of their books, so the account-weighted mean supplier loss rate IS this rate exactly. Switching is concentrated in engaged households, which makes individual suppliers differ from each other — it does not lower the mean. A book of average engagement loses at this rate.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
The reason distribution exists for SWITCHERS only. Nothing published that this pass could find gives the rate at which each cause fires across the whole population — which is what a model of departures actually needs. Converting a stated-reason share among movers into a cause-specific hazard over everybody requires an assumption, and that assumption is not in the published record.

There is no published series for what proportion of households LOOKED and did not move. Intent to switch is surveyed; comparison-without-action is not, or not in a form this pass located. That population matters more than its size suggests, because it is the one a retention offer can actually reach.

The fixed-to-variable spread over the 2016–2025 record is only partly published. February 2025 (£140 below the cap) and the qualitative direction in 2022 (fixed above the cap) are both firm; a continuous quarterly series of cheapest-fixed against cap across the whole window was not found in this pass and would be worth having, because it is the single driver behind take-up.

Home moves are absent from this page entirely. A move onto a deemed contract is one of the three ways a household arrives on a variable tariff, it is a large flow in a country with roughly a million housing transactions a year plus a much larger rental churn, and no source consulted here quantifies the deemed-contract inflow.

And the exit-fee minority is characterised but not located. Ofgem reports that 17% disproportionately prioritise exit fees; nothing published says who they are, which means the segment cannot be predicted from anything a supplier observes.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not establish a set of cause weights to draw departures from. The published reason distribution is over movers, and the honest output is the SHAPE — price dominant, service a real and substantial second, contractual events dominant for business — together with an explicit statement that turning that into a hazard requires an assumption this page cannot source.

It does not establish how many households are highly elastic. That is a curriculum value and belongs to the director; what this page contributes is the published finding that price WEIGHT varies far less between subgroups than intuition suggests, which is an argument for a narrow distribution and against a wide one.

It does not cover the channel through which a household sees an alternative, or the price it is shown when it looks. That is a separate mechanism with its own published record and it has its own page.

And it does not, by itself, change any code. What it does is make a specific class of future mistake visible: any tariff-type share, switching rate or departure reason that appears in this repository without a source can now be held against a page that says what the published evidence supports and, more usefully, what it does not.

meta.title: The price a household is shown, and why it is not the price it pays
meta.subtitle: A comparison site and the price cap headline both quote a year's money at a consumption you probably don't have, for a tariff whose rate may not last the year. The household is comparing a real forward price against an implied one nobody is offering.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem State of the Market Report, energy retail markets highlights (published April 2025); Ofgem Confidence Code for domestic price comparison websites, revised code in force from end-March 2015; CMA Energy Market Investigation 2016, Appendix 9.10; PCW and broker commission anchors held at docs/market_research/B2_CATEGORY6_CAC_ANCHORS.md

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Both the price cap headline and every comparison-site listing quote an ANNUAL figure at a standard assumed consumption — 2,700 kWh of electricity and 11,500 kWh of gas a year — which displays a variable tariff as though today's rate will hold for twelve months, so a household choosing between a fixed offer and its current variable deal is comparing a real forward price against an implied forward price that nobody has offered and nobody is committed to.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
When Ofgem says the cap is £1,849, that is not a bill and not a cap on your bill. It is the annual cost, at the capped unit rates and standing charge, for a household using the typical amounts of gas and electricity, paying by direct debit. Use more and you pay more; there is no ceiling on the total.

The same convention runs through every comparison. A fixed tariff quoted at £1,700 a year and a variable tariff quoted at £1,849 a year look like two prices for the same thing. They are not. The first is a commitment: that unit rate is what you will pay for the term. The second is an EXTRAPOLATION: it is today's rate multiplied out over a year, and the rate will change at the next cap period, upward or downward, and nobody has promised otherwise.

So the comparison flatters whichever side the cap happens to lag. In a rising market the cap sits below where costs have already gone, so the variable quote is too low and fixed deals look expensive — which is exactly what households saw in 2022, when they declined fixed offers priced above the cap and were mostly wrong to. In a falling market the cap sits above where costs have gone, the variable quote is too high, and fixed deals look better than they are.

None of this is a trick. It is the only convention that lets two tariffs be shown side by side at all. But it means the number driving the decision is neither what the household would pay on the variable tariff nor what it would pay on the fixed one; it is a third, constructed number, and it has its own errors.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE QUOTING CONVENTION. Ofgem's Typical Domestic Consumption Values are 2,700 kWh of electricity and 11,500 kWh of gas per year, and the headline cap figure is those volumes priced at the capped unit rate plus the standing charge. In April 2025 that produced £1,849 for a direct debit dual-fuel household, £1,803 for prepayment and £1,969 for standard credit — three headline numbers for the same underlying cap, differing only by payment method. A household whose consumption differs from the typical values sees a headline that is wrong for it by roughly the same proportion, in both directions at once if its gas and electricity use diverge.

WHAT SITS INSIDE THAT NUMBER. For a dual-fuel direct debit standard variable tariff over April to June 2025, Ofgem's breakdown was 45% wholesale costs, 20% network costs, 13% operating costs, 11% policy costs, 6% other costs and 5% VAT. Only the first of those is what most people think they are shopping for.

WHAT A COMPARISON SITE IS. Ofgem operates a voluntary accreditation scheme, the Confidence Code, for domestic price comparison sites. An accredited site must be independent of suppliers, must cover the whole market including all payment methods, and must display all available tariffs unless the customer actively chooses to see fewer — with the wording of that choice tested with consumers for clarity. It must make its commission arrangements transparent and explain plainly that it earns commission on the tariffs a customer can switch to through the site. It must also run a complaints procedure and link to energy efficiency information and government grant schemes. The revised code took effect at the end of March 2015.

Those requirements exist because of the obvious conflict: a comparison site is paid per switch by the supplier the customer moves to, so its incentive is to produce a switch, and its accreditation is what constrains it to show the tariffs it is not paid for alongside the ones it is.

WHAT THE CHANNEL COSTS, AND WHY THE CHANNELS ARE NOT COMPARABLE. A comparison site earns roughly £25 to £30 per fuel switched — a per-switch commission, the same however much the customer goes on to consume. A business broker is paid completely differently: an ongoing per-unit adder embedded in the customer's own unit rate for the life of the contract, typically 0.5 to 2.0 pence per kWh for a small business and less for larger sites, so a broker-introduced customer costs nothing at signup and costs more the more they use. Direct and brand acquisition has no published GB-energy benchmark at all. These are three different KINDS of money and a single cost-per-acquisition constant cannot represent them.

WHAT THE MARKET LOOKS LIKE FROM THE OTHER SIDE. There were 23 active domestic suppliers and 72 active business suppliers as of Ofgem's April 2025 reporting, with the six largest holding 91% of the domestic market. So the listing a household sees is long, and the outcome is concentrated.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
The shown price and the paid price should DIVERGE, systematically and with a sign that depends on where the cap sits relative to costs. Any model in which a household responds to the true differential is a model of a household with information no household has.

That divergence should be largest exactly when it matters most. In a fast-rising market the extrapolated variable quote understates what a variable customer will actually pay over the coming year, so the measured take-up of fixed deals should be LOWER than a true-cost comparison would predict, and the households who declined should turn out to have lost money. That is the 2022 pattern and it should emerge from the convention rather than being asserted.

A household's error should scale with how far its consumption is from typical. A high-consuming household is under-quoted in absolute pounds by any typical-consumption headline, so its true saving from switching is larger than the one it is shown — which means published savings figures systematically understate the prize for exactly the households with the most to gain.

Acquisition cost should not be one number. Per-switch for comparison sites, per-kWh over the term for brokers, unknown for direct. A book acquired through different channels should have a materially different cost profile over time even at the same headline volume.

And the number of tariffs on display should track the spread. When the cheapest deal sits far below the cap the listing is long and switching rises; when everything is at the cap the listing collapses to one row and switching goes to near zero, which is what 2021/22 was.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The typical domestic consumption values of 2,700 kWh electricity and 11,500 kWh gas, and the April 2025 cap headlines of £1,849 direct debit, £1,803 prepayment and £1,969 standard credit (Ofgem State of the Market, April 2025). The April–June 2025 bill breakdown for a dual-fuel direct debit SVT: 45% wholesale, 20% network, 13% operating, 11% policy, 6% other, 5% VAT (same source). The Confidence Code's accreditation requirements on independence, whole-of-market coverage, tariff display, commission transparency, complaints and efficiency information (Ofgem, revised code effective end-March 2015). Supplier counts of 23 domestic and 72 non-domestic, and a 91% domestic share for the six largest (Ofgem, April 2025). Comparison-site commission of roughly £25–£30 per fuel and broker trails of 0.2–2.0 pence per kWh by size band (as held at docs/market_research/B2_CATEGORY6_CAC_ANCHORS.md).

WHAT IS NOT KNOWABLE FROM THE PUBLIC RECORD. The per-customer acquisition costs the six large suppliers reported to the CMA are redacted in the published appendix, so no supplier-specific GB acquisition cost exists at all. No comparison site publishes a rate card. The commission figures above are cited from secondary commentary on a CMA-era rate and are very unlikely to be uniform across suppliers, since they are commercially negotiated.

WHAT IS ASSERTED HERE AND IS NOT A PUBLISHED FIGURE. That the quoting convention biases the fixed-versus-variable comparison, and in which direction, is a DEDUCTION from the convention and the cap's backward-looking observation window, not a finding anyone has published as such. It is stated as a mechanism because the mechanism follows from two published facts; it is not stated as a measurement, and no number is attached to it on this page.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
No published quarterly series of the cheapest available fixed tariff against the cap across 2016–2025 was located in this pass. February 2025's £140 differential and the qualitative 2022 inversion are both firm; the continuous series that would let the convention's bias be MEASURED rather than deduced is not in hand.

The share of switches arriving through each channel is held here at moderate confidence from secondary sources, and no primary Ofgem or supplier series was located that breaks GB domestic switches down by acquisition route. The concentration figure among comparison sites has the same provenance.

What a comparison site actually displays by DEFAULT — the ordering, the number of rows above the fold, whether savings are shown against the cap or against the customer's own current tariff — is not in the Confidence Code text consulted here, and it is very likely the part that most affects behaviour. The code constrains what must be AVAILABLE; it says less about what is prominent.

Nothing here quantifies how many households compare on a site and then buy direct from the supplier, which is a known pattern and would mean the channel that produced the switch and the channel that was paid for it are different.

And the retention channel is not covered at all. A retention offer is shown to an existing customer through the supplier's own route, is not on any comparison site, and its terms are not published — which is why the acquisition-and-retention page treats retention as foregone margin rather than as a channel with a price.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not establish a number for the gap between the shown price and the paid price. It establishes that a gap exists by construction, states its sign in each market condition, and stops there, because measuring it needs the quarterly cheapest-fixed series that this pass did not find.

It does not establish channel shares that could be drawn from. The channel taxonomy — comparison site, direct, affiliate, broker, doorstep, retention — is real and the cost STRUCTURES differ in kind; the SHARES are not established here at a confidence that would justify treating them as marginals.

It does not cover the cost of serving a customer once won, bad debt, or the cost of losing one. Those sit in the same neighbourhood and belong to other pages.

And it deliberately does not restate the acquisition and retention cost model, which already has its own page. What is new here is the DISPLAY — what the household is shown, by whom, under what accreditation, and on what convention — which is the half that was missing.

meta.title: What a customer is worth, and what actually drives it
meta.subtitle: Value is contribution multiplied by survival — which makes the drivers an order, not a list. Pays, then stays, then how big the margin bet is, then everything else.
meta.wall_placement: Commons and practitioner judgement. The market prices, the cap cost stack, the consumption bands and the switching rates are published and cited. The unit margins, contact costs and every loyalty effect are a practitioner's estimates from decades in GB supply, labelled as such wherever they appear. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page: the simulation's job is to test these claims, and where it disagrees the disagreement is a finding to explain, never a number to converge to.

claim_freshness.source: OVO/SSE and E.ON/OVO transaction prices as reported; Ofgem price cap cost allowances and the EBIT allowance; Ofgem Consumer Impacts of Market Conditions survey wave 6 switching rates by payment method; DESNZ typical domestic consumption values; DCC published charges. Practitioner estimates are marked in place.
claim_freshness.note: Written as a thesis to be tested, not as a result. Ten hypotheses are stated falsifiably in the expected-shape rung with the measurement that would refute each. Nothing on this page has yet been measured against this project's own book — that is the work it exists to direct, and this page will be struck through where the measurement disagrees.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A customer is worth the cash they contribute each year — revenue less every cost they personally cause — for as long as they stay, and because those two things MULTIPLY rather than add, the drivers fall into a strict order: does this household pay, does it stay, how big is the margin bet the house makes, and only then everything a supplier might sell it. The order matters more than any single number in it, because it reverses the sign of ordinary commercial instincts: for a customer whose contribution is negative, a longer life multiplies the loss, so churn becomes a benefit and loyalty-building becomes actively harmful.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Take an ordinary dual-fuel household. The supplier makes roughly £226 a year gross margin on them — about 12% of an £1,860 bill, which sits inside the 8–14% range real GB suppliers report. Out of that comes the cost of billing them and answering their calls (~£40), the debt they leave (~£25), and the cost of getting their volume forecast wrong (~£15). What is left, about £146 a year, is the contribution. Fixed overhead — head office, IT, the licence — is NOT charged to them: that is a company-level hurdle the whole book must clear, and charging a slice of it to each customer is how suppliers talk themselves into thinking a customer is unprofitable when they are not.

Multiply £146 by how long they stay. At the market churn rate of about 12% a year that is roughly eight years, and discounted it comes to about £690 before the cost of acquiring them, about £540 after. THE ONE EXTERNAL CHECK ON ALL OF THIS: OVO paid about £143 per customer for SSE's retail book in January 2020, and E.ON is reported to be paying about £150 per customer for OVO's in 2026. A buyer pays contribution value less its own capitalised overhead, so £690 of contribution against £100–130 of overhead per customer per year over a four-to-five-year payback prices at £150–200. The arithmetic reconciles to what the market actually paid, twice, six years apart — which is the strongest evidence that the cost stack above is roughly the right shape.

theory.heading: Why it works this way
theory.body:
THE MERIT ORDER. Because value is contribution multiplied by survival, the drivers are lexicographic:

1. DOES IT PAY? If yearly contribution is negative, everything else inverts. A stressed standard-credit household is worth about −£786 at 18% churn, −£517 at 40% and −£410 at 60%: churn is a BENEFIT. Give that household the value-added services and the loyalty they create, and it gets WORSE, because loyalty lengthens a negative stream. The rational treatment is to minimise exposure and not retain.

2. DOES IT STAY? And here the two things travel together: THE MECHANISM THAT MAKES PEOPLE LEAVE IS THE SAME MECHANISM THAT MAKES THEM TAKE THE DISCOUNTED DEAL. Price elasticity and churn are not independent drivers to be modelled separately — an engaged, price-sensitive household both shops around and takes the cheap tariff, so the combination 'excellent margin, high churn' barely exists in the wild. A big house on a discounted fixed deal at 30% churn is worth about £258; an ordinary loyal house at cap margin at 4% churn is worth about £762. The disengaged customer sitting on the standard tariff is not a failure of engagement to be corrected; on a lifetime view they are the engine, and the correct treatment is restraint.

3. HOW BIG IS THE BET, AND IS IT HEDGED? Gross margin is volume times unit margin, and those are separate things with an interaction. The house decides the SIZE of the bet; pricing and hedging decide its SIGN. The same large old house is worth about £1,200 on the cap well hedged and about −£4,700 under-hedged through a crisis. Volume is a lever on margin, not margin.

4. VALUE-ADD, LAST, and only where there is a controllable asset with permission to control it, or a loyalty effect to earn. On a house that pays and stays it is worth several hundred pounds; on a house that does not pay it is worth less than nothing.

expected_shape.heading: What we expect to find, stated so it can be refuted
expected_shape.body:
Ten claims, each with the measurement that would refute it. None has yet been tested against this project's own book; that is the point of writing them down first.

H1 — DEBT DOMINATES THE DOWNSIDE. Bad debt plus the cost to serve it explains more variance in fully-costed customer value than any other driver. Refuted if a variance decomposition on real draws puts debt and collections below 40% of downside variance.

H2 — CONSUMPTION DOMINATES THE UPSIDE, AND IT IS HOUSE PHYSICS. Size, fabric and heating fuel explain most of the positive tail. Refuted if the household sample explains more of the level variance than the housing sample.

H3 — ENGAGEMENT IS A MULTIPLIER, NOT AN ADDEND. The value of low churn scales with net contribution and is irrelevant on low-net customers. Refuted if the churn×net interaction term does not exceed either main effect.

H4 — VALUE-ADD EARNS THROUGH LOYALTY, NOT INCOME. Direct income from services is under £50/yr for more than 90% of customers; the churn reduction is worth more on any customer netting over £100/yr. Refuted by measuring the loyalty parameter rather than assuming it.

H5 — ACCURATE FORECASTING AND BILLING IS WORTH AS MUCH AS VALUE-ADD, POSSIBLY MORE. Right-sized direct debits, no bill shocks and a correctly-shaped hedge lower churn, contacts, debt and volume risk together. Refuted if a supplier forecasting on premise physics does not beat one forecasting on profile averages, in forecast risk, bill-shock churn and arrears.

H6 — THE APATHETIC ARE THE QUIET ENGINE AND THE RIGHT ACTION IS RESTRAINT. Refuted if the disengaged archetype does not rank near the top on lifetime value, or if unsolicited offers do not raise their churn.

H7 — CONTROLLABLE ASSETS WITH PERMISSION ARE THE ONLY LARGE VALUE-ADD UPSIDE. An EV and a battery with permission to control create £60–120/yr of shape value; SOLAR ALONE IS NEGATIVE TO THE SUPPLIER, because it removes volume and worsens shape. Refuted if the sign does not hold across weather regions.

H8 — NATURAL SHAPE IS WORTH A LITTLE, NOT A LOT. Ordinary variation in when a household uses energy is worth £10–20/yr. Refuted if the interquartile range falls outside ±£15.

H9 — SMART METERING PAYS THROUGH COLLECTABILITY, NOT THROUGH COST. This is the one most often got backwards. The metering cost difference between smart and traditional is tens of pounds a year in either direction and is not the point. What a smart meter buys is the OPTION to move a household that will not pay — as distinct from cannot pay, and where no vulnerability protection applies — onto pay-as-you-go. That single option is worth about £840 on the stressed standard-credit household: it moves them from roughly −£786 to about break-even. Hundreds of pounds, against tens. Refuted by measuring bad-debt loss by meter type holding payment method and income stress constant.

H10 — THE AVERAGE RECONCILES TO THE MARKET. A book drawn in population proportion averages £600–700 of contribution value before acquisition cost, netting to the market's £150 after a buyer's overhead. Refuted if it does not land near £150 — in which case the cost stack is wrong before any of the drivers matter.

live_evidence.heading: What we can show today
live_evidence.body:
Nothing on this page has been measured against this project's own simulated book yet, and saying so is more useful than a figure that looks measured.

What IS externally anchored and cited: the two transaction prices (£143 per customer, OVO/SSE 2020; ~£150, E.ON/OVO 2026 as reported); the price cap's cost allowances and its EBIT allowance, which set the unit-margin order of magnitude; DESNZ typical domestic consumption values for the 2,700 kWh electricity and 11,500 kWh gas bands; DCC's published charges; and Ofgem's Consumer Impacts of Market Conditions survey, which puts annual switching at 5.6% for direct debit, 5.7% for standard credit and 3.1% for prepayment — the observable behind the engagement claims in the theory rung.

What is a practitioner's estimate and NOT a published figure: the unit margins per fuel and the standing-charge margin; third-party per-meter costs beyond DCC; contact costs and contact rates; the magnitude of forecast and volume risk; shape values; value-add income and installation margins; and every loyalty effect, which is a hypothesis by construction — nobody publishes the churn reduction caused by a service, because no supplier runs the counterfactual.

The reference model behind these numbers computes explicit yearly cash flows over ten years with a tenure-dependent churn hazard and a terminal value, rather than multiplying a constant contribution by an average lifetime. That distinction is not cosmetic: the shortcut undervalues loyal customers badly, because a terminal value adds about 41% to a 4%-churn customer and about 2% to a 28%-churn one — so truncating at ten years biases against exactly the customers this thesis says are the engine.

residuals.heading: What we do not know, and what would settle it
residuals.body:
THE GAPS, stated rather than filled.

The discount rate is a placeholder at 8% and has no source here; it belongs to whoever sets this project's direction, not to the analyst.

The terminal-value method — a decaying perpetuity on the customer's own churn rather than a market multiple — is a choice with a real alternative, and it is not settled.

The can't-pay/won't-pay split is the single most load-bearing unpublished quantity on this page. H9's entire £840 turns on it: pay-as-you-go conversion is legitimate for a household that will not pay and is protected for one that cannot, and no published source separates them at household level. It has been looked for three times. Until it is established it stays an explicitly empty slot with a named reason, because a plausible number here would be read as established within a week.

The household-level switching amplitude — how hard a given household responds to a given saving — is likewise unpublished at the resolution this needs.

Every loyalty effect is a hypothesis, not an estimate with error bars.

And the largest structural gap: this page describes what drives value for a supplier that already has a customer. It says almost nothing about how you FIND the households worth having in the first place, which is the harder problem and the one this project exists to answer.

scope_delta.heading: How this connects to the rest
scope_delta.body:
This page is the frame the household, housing and weather work is being built to test. Its merit order says where fidelity effort is worth spending: payment, collections and vulnerability first, because that is where the largest per-customer swing sits and where a badly-managed household costs more than a well-managed one earns; then how households move home, because renters churn by MOVING rather than by switching and a supplier that models only switching is blind to a third of its real dynamics; then bill accuracy and the shape of the year; then portfolio forecasting and hedging; and last the assets and the permission to control them.

It connects to the acquisition and retention economics page, which carries what it costs to win a customer — the £150 that this page's arithmetic nets against. It connects to how households choose, which carries the engagement and switching behaviour the second rung of the merit order depends on. And it connects to the price cap page, which sets the unit margins that decide whether the volume bet described here pays or costs.

What this page must not become: a target. Every figure here is a prediction about a world that has not been measured yet. When the measurement disagrees, the disagreement is the finding — the mechanism is wrong, the anchor is wrong, or this thesis is wrong — and the honest move is to strike the claim through and say which.

meta.title: How many synthetic households represent Britain
meta.subtitle: You cannot simulate 28 million homes. You do not have to. But the number you do need is decided by something less obvious than how varied Britain is.
meta.one_line: A synthetic book stands in for a real one when it reproduces the distribution of what customers actually do. How many households that takes depends on what KIND of thing you add to it: a stratum that behaves by different rules multiplies the count, a correlated axis is nearly free, and a driver that moves households along quantities already being measured does nothing at all. The full vector currently needs 8,822 deliberately-chosen, weighted households against a reference population of 120,000 — and that figure is still rising with the size of the reference, so it is not yet settled.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons and method. The evidence is published — DESNZ NEED, Census 2021 and 2022, HadUK-Grid. The sampling method is general statistics, not a simulation internal. The figures quoted are this project's own measurements and are labelled as such.

claim_freshness.source: DESNZ NEED anonymised 2026 sample (50,000 dwellings, England and Wales); Census 2021 TS017/TS041; Scotland's Census 2022 UV402; HadUK-Grid 1 km climate normals; ONS UPRN Directory.
claim_freshness.route: Measured directly: tools/demand_vector_coverage.py, tools/billing_axis_coverage.py, tools/stock_joint_generator.py, tools/people_physical_layer.py. Every figure on this page is reproducible from those and named beside its claim.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body:
A sample of synthetic households represents a country when the DISTRIBUTION of what they do matches the real one, not when the sample looks like a scale model of the population. A chosen-and-weighted sample beats a random one by a large factor, because it can put households where the variation is and carry a weight saying how many real homes each one stands for.

ON THE FULL VECTOR THE CURRENT FIGURE IS 8,822 HOUSEHOLDS, measured against a reference population of 120,000 and required to match it to within five percentage points everywhere. That is not a settled answer and this page does not present it as one. The figure still grows with the size of the reference it is scored against: 6,816 against a 20,000-household reference, 8,822 against 120,000. What is published here is a measurement with a named limit rather than a size.

An earlier version of this page led with 243. That figure is real, but it is the PARTIAL vector — the heat-driven axes alone, before annual electricity, the half-hourly shape and the payment-method stratum were in it. It was published as a floor and it behaved like one.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Imagine you must describe Britain's housing to someone using a hundred example homes.

The instinct is to make them REPRESENTATIVE. If 19% of homes are flats, make 19 of them flats. That is a scale model, and it wastes almost all of your hundred on homes that are much like each other. The ordinary semi is already well understood: a supplier's segment model handles it and the customer gets a reasonable outcome.

The alternative is to choose homes because they are DIFFERENT from each other — the off-gas bungalow on a Welsh hillside, the Edinburgh tenement flat, the large uninsulated detached house — and then attach a number to each saying how many real homes it stands for. The examples are deliberately unusual; the WEIGHTS carry the representativeness.

That inversion is the whole method. THE SAMPLE IS DENSEST WHERE THE POPULATION IS THINNEST, because the uncommon combinations are exactly the ones an averaging model rounds to the nearest segment and gets wrong. Aggregate anything — revenue, carbon, arrears — and the weights restore the true mass.

Both halves are needed. Choose without weighting and your totals are nonsense. Weight without choosing and you are back to a scale model, which is what a random sample already gives you.

theory.heading: Why the count depends on strata, not on variety
theory.body:
The natural guess is that the number of households you need grows with how varied Britain is. It does not, in any simple way. What matters is which of three kinds of thing you are adding.

A STRATUM MULTIPLIES THE COUNT. A stratum is a group whose response differs in kind. A home heated by electricity is not a gas-heated home that happens to use less gas: it has a different heat source, a different bill, a different exposure to weather and a different response to a price change. A sample must span each stratum in its own right, so strata compose multiplicatively. And the binding cost is the SMALLEST CELL of the cross rather than the number of cells — electrically heated households not on direct debit are 5.7% of the book, and they must be reproduced as thoroughly as the largest group.

A CORRELATED AXIS IS NEARLY FREE. Weather sensitivity, how much a home's demand moves with temperature, is largely determined by the fabric that already sets its annual total. The households already chosen to span the totals mostly span the sensitivities too.

A DRIVER DOES NOTHING, and this one is counter-intuitive enough that we predicted it wrong. A driver is something that changes how households behave without adding a quantity the sample is scored on. Occupancy is the clearest case. How many people live in a home genuinely drives its hot-water use, and wiring that in moved the modelled gas total measurably closer to metered reality. It changed the sample size by three households in 6,816, against a 20,000-household reference. The reason is that the acceptance test scores seven output quantities and occupancy is not one of them: it moves households around inside a shape that was already being reproduced.

So the useful question when someone proposes adding detail is not how much variation does this add. It is whether the thing splits the population into groups that behave differently, adds a quantity the sample must span, or merely moves households along quantities already being measured.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body:
If the mechanism above is right, five things follow. Each has now been tested and one of them failed.

ADDING A STRATUM SHOULD MULTIPLY THE COUNT. Confirmed, and understated. Doubling the strata, from fuel alone to fuel crossed with payment method, multiplied the requirement thirty-seven fold rather than two-fold. The reasoning was right and the arithmetic was too kind: coverage is owed within every cell, so the cost is set by the smallest one rather than by how many there are.

ADDING A CORRELATED AXIS SHOULD BARELY MOVE IT. Confirmed. Weather sensitivity moved the count from 273 to 243.

ADDING GEOGRAPHY SHOULD BE CHEAP where it is more of an existing condition than a new behaviour. Confirmed. Including Scotland, the coldest eight per cent of British homes and previously excluded outright, moved the count from 275 to 273. Colder is not a new behaviour; it is more of an existing one.

A CHOSEN-AND-WEIGHTED SAMPLE SHOULD BEAT A RANDOM ONE BY A LARGE FACTOR. Confirmed, and it is a falsifiable check rather than a hope: if the two come out at the same scale, the weighting is doing no work and the design has quietly reverted to representativeness.

ADDING AN AXIS INDEPENDENT OF FABRIC AND WEATHER SHOULD RAISE THE COUNT TWO TO FOUR FOLD. REFUTED. Occupancy is independent of fabric and weather, and it moved the count by four hundredths of one per cent. The prediction confused a driver with an axis. Only what the sample is scored on can move the number, and being independent of the things that were already in the vector is not the same as being in it.

And the honest counterpart to all five: a figure quoted without naming what is missing from it is not a size, it is a floor.

live_evidence.heading: The evidence, measured
live_evidence.body:
THE HISTORY OF THE NUMBER, AND EVERY FIGURE CARRIES WHAT IT WAS MEASURED AGAINST. Two of these were quoted side by side before anyone noticed they were on different clocks, so each is given here with its reference population and its tolerance.

Against a reference of 120,000 households at a five-point tolerance, the requirement was 13 for annual gas alone; 8,500 once electricity and the non-gas stratum went in, drawn at random; 275 for the same vector once the sample was chosen and weighted rather than drawn; 273 after Scotland was included; and 243 after weather sensitivity was added. Everything up to that point is the PARTIAL vector. With annual electricity, the half-hourly shape and the payment-method stratum in it, the same measurement at the same reference and the same tolerance gives 8,822. THAT COMPARISON IS THE HONEST ONE — 243 to 8,822 is a thirty-six fold rise, and the only thing that changed is what the vector contains.

THE FIGURE HAS NOT CONVERGED, and a second series at deliberately smaller references is what shows it. At a ten-point tolerance the count was 2,716 against a 12,000-household reference and 3,824 against 40,000. At the stricter five-point tolerance it was 6,816 against 20,000 and 8,822 against 120,000. The two tolerances are not comparable to one another, but within each of them the count rises with the reference. The ratio of sample to reference is the thing to watch: against 20,000 the sample was 34% of the population it was reproducing, which is barely a compression at all, while against 120,000 it is 7.4%.

THE STRATUM EVIDENCE. Adding electricity together with the 18.5% of British homes not heated by gas multiplied the requirement roughly sevenfold. That group is not a variation on gas heating; it is a different way of being a customer. Adding payment method on top multiplied it again, by thirty-seven.

THE DRIVER EVIDENCE, WHICH REFUTED A PREDICTION. Domestic hot water is genuinely driven by how many people live in a home: the United Kingdom's own regulatory dwelling model puts daily hot-water volume at 36 litres plus 25 per occupant, and a metered study of 45,000 homes agrees with that to within seven per cent at the average occupancy. Wiring it in moved the modelled gas total from 0.883 times the metered reality for the same households to 0.992 times, closing about nine tenths of the gap (0.109 of the 0.117 shortfall). It moved the sample size from 6,813 to 6,816, both against the same 20,000-household reference and the same tolerance, so the comparison is attributable. We had predicted a two-to-four-fold rise, on the reasoning that occupancy is independent of fabric and weather. That was true and it was irrelevant.

THE GEOGRAPHY EVIDENCE. Scotland is the coldest eight per cent of British homes and had been excluded outright, because the survey the stock was drawn from covers England and Wales only. Including it moved the count from 275 to 273. It did change the world it is measured in: from 143,511 to 194,865 populated one-kilometre weather cells, and from 24.7 to 27.1 million households.

THE DESIGN EVIDENCE. On the partial vector, against the same 120,000-household reference and the same five-point tolerance, a random sample needs 5,400 households where a chosen-and-weighted one needs 243. That is a factor of twenty-two, and both pass exactly the same test. The comparison is also the design's own tell: if the two ever come out at the same scale, the weighting has stopped doing any work.

HOW REPRODUCING THE DISTRIBUTION IS TESTED. Every axis, and 64 random combinations of axes, must have an empirical distribution within five percentage points of the population's everywhere, which is about half a decile. The 64 combinations are the point: testing each axis separately cannot see whether the JOINT is right, and two homes with identical consumption but opposite retrofit headroom differ only in the joint. The weights are solved on a different set of directions from the ones the acceptance scores, so a design that passed only on what it was fitted to would be caught.

WHAT THE SAMPLE IS NOT SIZED FOR, NOW MEASURED AXIS BY AXIS RATHER THAN ASSUMED. A household is more than what it uses: it has a meter and a read pattern, a payment method, a tariff with its dates, a move history and a credit position, and those are the things that make a bill right or wrong. Two homes with identical consumption, one read quarterly on an estimate and one settled half-hourly, are entirely different to bill and to serve. On all five of those axes this sample is NOT SIZED, and the answer has a different shape on each.

FOUR OF THE FIVE ARE ABSENT FROM THE SAMPLE ALTOGETHER — meter type and read pattern, tariff and its dates, move history, and credit position. Nothing in the sample carries them, so no figure about them exists at any sample size and no larger sample would produce one. They are UNCOUNTED DIMENSIONS of the count above, published here rather than left for a reader to notice.

THE FIFTH, PAYMENT METHOD, IS CARRIED AND STILL NOT SPANNED, for two reasons with different cures. It carries two categories where the world has three: direct debit is published at 72 per cent of standard electricity customers, and the split of the remaining 28 per cent between prepayment and standard credit is not published in the source we hold, so it has not been invented. And the sample DRAWS payment method from that same 72 per cent, so its coming out at 72.1 per cent is arithmetic rather than evidence — it is what the sample was built to do, and saying otherwise would be publishing a check that cannot fail. What the sample size does buy on that axis is a bound: at a 20,000-household sample the direct-debit share is pinned to within 0.6 percentage points, and 310 households would have been enough to pin it to the five-point tolerance used throughout this page.

SO THE COUNT ABOVE IS A FLOOR FOR A SECOND REASON, ON TOP OF THE ONE ALREADY STATED. Meter read pattern and credit position are strata rather than correlated axes, and the one stratum this page has already added multiplied the requirement thirty-seven fold. The census is tools/billing_axis_coverage.py --measure, and it refuses to run at all if the canon's list of axes gains one it has not been taught.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
8,822 IS A MEASUREMENT WITH THREE NAMED LIMITS, NOT THE SIZE OF THE BOOK.

THE FIRST LIMIT IS THAT IT HAS NOT CONVERGED. The figure grows with the reference population it is scored against: 6,816 against 20,000 households and 8,822 against 120,000. Settling it needs a larger reference rather than another axis, which is a tractable engineering problem rather than an open modelling question, but it is not yet done.

THE SECOND LIMIT IS THAT THE VECTOR DECLARES SEVEN AXES AND CARRIES FIVE. Three of the seven are the same direction. The seasonal-swing axis is an exact linear rescaling of the weather-sensitivity axis, and the thermostat turn-down ceiling is a third scaled copy of the same heat-loss coefficient; their mutual correlations are 1.000000 and 0.999997, by construction rather than by coincidence. Only three directions carry more than one per cent of the variance. Dropping one of the duplicates cut the count by 31%, SO PART OF THE PUBLISHED FIGURE IS AN ARTEFACT OF THE INSTRUMENT RATHER THAN A PROPERTY OF BRITAIN. The seasonal-swing axis in particular is not currently a real quantity at all: the share of annual demand falling in the coldest half of the year cannot be computed by a model that simulates only the first of October to the thirty-first of March.

THE THIRD LIMIT IS WHAT IS STILL OUTSIDE THE VECTOR, and the mechanism above now sorts it into things that will matter and things that will not. Meter read pattern and arrears position are STRATA and should multiply the count. A real seasonal-shape axis would be a genuinely new direction, and it is where occupancy would finally show up, because a five-person household's gas is flatter across the year than a single person's in the same dwelling. Move history is a driver and should do nothing. Credit position is correlated with arrears and should be small. What a tariff is and when it started is partly a stratum and its effect is unknown.

HOUSEHOLD SHAPE IS MODELLED AND NOT VALIDATED. The only public household-level load shape for Great Britain is a single population-average curve on a 1997 reference year. A validated source exists but is gated behind accredited access and has not been pursued.

THE MODEL IS VALIDATED AGAINST THE METERS ONLY AT THE LEVEL OF THE TOTAL. Modelled gas is 0.992 times the observed metered gas for the same households, up from 0.883 before domestic hot water was modelled at all. That is a check on the total and not on its shape.

WHAT THE WEATHER ARCHIVE COVERS, AND WHAT THAT BOUNDS. Every household here is placed in a real one-kilometre weather cell, and there are 194,865 populated ones. But the weather those cells carry is a THIRTY-YEAR MONTHLY NORMAL — a typical January, not the January of 2022. Real DAILY weather exists for four locations only: London, Manchester, Glasgow and a Cotswolds site. Measured against the drivers that matter, those four cover 20.4% of British households on winter temperature, 27.8% on wind and 17.3% on sunshine — and only 2.0% on all three at once.

That bounds two different things and it is worth separating them. The SAMPLE SIZE on this page is computed from monthly normals and is not limited by the archive: reproducing a distribution of annual demand does not need to know what any particular Tuesday was like. Anything needing SUB-DAILY physics is limited to those four locations — how a house actually responds to a cold snap, what a thermostat change saves on a given day, how demand moves within an hour.

WE COULD CLOSE THAT GAP BY INVENTING THE WEATHER and we have decided not to. Generating plausible daily series for the other 194,861 cells from their monthly averages would make every figure on this page look better-founded and would put a fabricated observable underneath all of them — a number that reads as measured and is not. The honest position is that the geographic reach of the sample and the geographic reach of the sub-daily physics are different numbers, and this page publishes both rather than the flattering one.

SCOTLAND'S STOCK IS RAKED AND NOT OBSERVED. The fabric joint is fitted on England and Wales, because the survey covers only those, and moved onto Scotland's own census shares for property type. That carry-over is an assumption, and it is a smaller one than pretending the Scottish stock is English.

scope_delta.heading: Scope and honesty
scope_delta.body:
WHAT IS GENERAL AND WHAT IS OURS. The method — choose for difference, weight for mass, test the distribution — is standard statistics and transfers to any synthetic population. The specific numbers are this project's measurements on British housing evidence and carry its assumptions.

EVERY FIGURE HERE IS REPRODUCIBLE. The command tools/demand_vector_coverage.py --measure produces the counts and curves; tools/stock_joint_generator.py --measure the plausibility and Scottish figures; tools/people_physical_layer.py --split the address result.

THE UNCOUNTED AXES ARE ENUMERATED IN THE CODE and not only here, so the number cannot be quoted from the tool without the caveat travelling with it.

A RELATED FINDING, FROM THE SAME PROGRAMME. How much does a postcode tell you about who lives in a home? Across all 24.8 million households of England and Wales, an output area of about 130 homes explains 9% of the variation in household size. The other 91% must be discovered. Occupancy is something a supplier must meter rather than look up — which is the same conclusion this page reaches from the other end, since occupancy turned out to be a driver the sample size cannot see.

meta.title: What a house does to its energy use, and where the potential sits across Britain
meta.subtitle: Size, fabric and the fuel at the meter set most of what a home uses. Where it sits sets less than you would think. And the potential to save is not where the average home is.
meta.one_line: A British home's gas use is driven first by its size and the fabric that wraps it, then by whether it has a gas supply at all, and only then by where it is. Those quantities travel together — small homes are flats, old homes are leaky, rural homes are detached and off the gas — so a model that draws them one at a time invents one house in five that does not exist and misses the large detached homes where the money is. This project's sample of Britain's housing is chosen for difference rather than proportion: 233 houses reproduce 99% of the household-weighted variation in five measured outputs, but one of the five tails does not close at any affordable size, and the ceilings on solar, batteries, car charging and heating settings cannot yet be stated at all.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons and method. The published facts are from DESNZ's National Energy Efficiency Data-Framework (NEED) anonymised 2026 sample, the English Housing Survey, the Energy Follow-Up Survey 2017, MCS installation statistics and Met Office HadUK-Grid. The cross-tabulations of those sources (floor area against gas, fuel by property type, how strongly the attributes travel together, deprivation within a size band) are this project's own computations on published data. The sample size, the five output measures, the corners and the tail coverage are this project's own measurements of its own model and are labelled as such wherever they appear. Nothing here is what any supplier, including this one, can see of a particular home.
meta.no_current_level: The sample size and coverage figures are readings of this project's own model of Britain's housing, measured 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-08. They describe the method's current state, not a target, and they will change as the model gains the quantities it is missing. The published facts do not change with the model.
