headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB supplier must take all reasonable steps to read every credit meter once a year. It has a legal power to enter to read the meter, but it cannot use that power against a refusal without a magistrate's warrant. It must look for theft, but each theft it finds costs it money, because theft nobody finds is shared across all suppliers by market share.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Reading the meter is the supplier's job. The rules ask it to try to get a reading at least once a year. A reading the customer sends in counts, and so does one a smart meter sends by itself. Until April 2016 there was also a rule to inspect every meter every two years. Ofgem removed it, because the yearly reading rule and safety law did the job better.

A customer does not break any law by refusing to let a meter reader in. The supplier has a legal right to come in at reasonable times. But without the occupier's consent, that right can only be used with a warrant from a magistrate. In practice warrants are used for suspected theft, for safety, and (until 2023, and on tighter rules since) to fit prepayment meters for debt. They are not used just to read a meter.

The access question matters because of the 12-month back-billing limit. A supplier normally cannot bill for energy used more than 12 months ago. The limit does not apply if the customer was obstructive: for example, they stole energy, or kept refusing a meter reader after reasonable requests. Simply not sending in readings does not count. The supplier has to show it asked.

Theft is the other half of the page. Every supplier must detect, investigate and prevent theft, and treat vulnerable households carefully when it does. But theft nobody finds never shows up on any one supplier's meters. Its cost is shared across all suppliers through the settlement system. Theft a supplier does find, it must pay for in settlement, and it usually recovers only a fraction from the person who stole it. That is why an industry incentive scheme pays suppliers for each detection.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE READ DUTY. Standard licence condition 21B.4 in both fuels has applied since 31 December 2014. It requires 'all reasonable steps to obtain a meter reading (including any meter reading transmitted electronically from a meter … or provided by the Customer) … at least once every year'. Prepayment meters are exempt. It is a duty of effort, not a guarantee. In electricity a second pressure comes from settlement. The Balancing and Settlement Code expects at least 97% of non-half-hourly energy to be settled on actual reads by the final run, 14 months on, and charges suppliers that fall short. The two-yearly inspection conditions were repealed from 1 April 2016. Ofgem's reason was that 21B.4 meets 'the objectives of billing accuracy in a more effective and efficient way than a static meter inspection interval'.

ENTRY. Electricity Act 1989 Schedule 6 paragraph 7(2) and Gas Act 1986 Schedule 2B paragraph 23(2) let a supplier's authorised officer enter 'at all reasonable times' to read or inspect a meter. Obstructing that power is an offence, with a fine of up to level 3. But the Rights of Entry (Gas and Electricity Boards) Act 1954 says no such right can be used without the occupier's consent or a warrant, except in an emergency. It also says nobody can be penalised just for refusing entry to someone who has no warrant. A magistrate grants a warrant if admission is reasonably required, the operator would otherwise be entitled to enter, and notice was given. The current court directions require 10 business days' notice for theft, safety or tamper applications and 15 for debt.

OBSTRUCTION AND BACK-BILLING. SLC 21BA.2(c) lifts the 12-month limit where the supplier could not bill correctly 'due to obstructive or manifestly unreasonable behaviour'. Ofgem's 2018 decision gives two examples: stealing energy, and not letting a meter reader in 'without good reason' after reasonable requests. It says 'we do not consider a consumer to be obstructive … when he or she does not supply a meter reading'. It also says the supplier's backstop is to 'take a meter reading themselves', and that suppliers must keep evidence.

THEFT DUTIES. SLC 12A has applied to gas since January 2013 and to electricity since July 2014. It requires all reasonable steps to detect, investigate and prevent theft, and membership of the industry Theft Arrangement, now Schedule 7 of the Retail Energy Code. Paragraph 12A.11 sets the standards a supplier must meet. It must find out whether the household includes someone of pensionable age, disabled or chronically sick, or who would struggle to pay. It must set instalments the household can afford, and offer a prepayment meter before cutting off supply. It must take all reasonable steps not to cut off vulnerable households in winter. It must show, on the balance of probabilities, that the theft was the customer's intentional act or culpable negligence before asking them to pay. REC Schedule 7 provides three things. TRAS is a shared risk-scoring service. A tip-off service requires the supplier to read each tip within 10 working days. The Theft Detection Incentive Scheme sets each supplier a detection target by market share and pays a set value per detection.

WHO PAYS. Theft nobody detects is never metered, so it never lands on the thief's supplier. In electricity it is smeared across suppliers by market share through GSP group correction. In gas it is part of Unidentified Gas, which has run at about 2.5% of throughput since 2017. When a supplier detects a theft, it enters the assessed energy into settlement, pays for it, and bills the customer. Ofgem's 2014 model assumed only 20-30% of those charges are recovered.

HALF-HOURLY SETTLEMENT FOR EVERYONE (MHHS). In April 2021 Ofgem decided that every electricity meter point will be settled half-hourly, with the final reconciliation run at four months instead of fourteen and the dispute run at twenty months instead of twenty-eight. The new central systems went live on 24 September 2025, suppliers began moving meters on 22 October 2025, every meter is due to have moved by 7 May 2027, and the switch to the four-month timetable is planned for 2 July 2027. Gas is not part of it. Meters that are not read remotely stay in, and their readings are turned into half-hourly figures by a central load-shaping service. Ofgem did not add a duty to read traditional meters more often: it said manual readings 'should be the exception' and left it to the settlement code's performance targets to allow for the traditional meters that remain. Energy still unread at four months is spread across all suppliers through group correction. The licence's once-a-year reading duty is unchanged.

WHAT FOUR MONTHS DOES TO UNBILLED ENERGY. Today a supplier whose estimate was too low pays for the difference in settlement whenever a reading arrives within fourteen months, but may only bill twelve months of it, so energy twelve to fourteen months old is paid for and cannot be billed. Under the four-month timetable that band disappears, and a new one appears: energy four to twelve months old can still be billed to the customer, but is no longer re-settled to the supplier; its cost is shared across the market. That is our derivation from the decision and the back-billing rule; nobody has published its size.

DO HARD-TO-READ METERS CLUSTER? The evidence says yes in kind, and is silent on how much. In the English Housing Survey 2022-23, 57% of private renters and 44% of owner occupiers reported no electricity smart meter (68% and 55% for gas), and households paying on receipt of a bill were less likely to have one than those paying by direct debit. Every cause of persistent no-access that suppliers put to Ofgem is a trait of the building or the landlord: a locked cupboard whose key the landlord holds, a bank of meters in a block of flats, a bill sent to the building company. The same buildings are harder to fit with working smart meters: Alt HAN Co says a home-network range problem affects over 700,000 households, and crowded shared meter rooms block installation. No source links no-access to vulnerability.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Reads: most credit meters read within a year, and a small group stays unread for years. In 2017 about 7% of domestic consumers had no bill based on a reading in 12 months. 97% of electricity energy is settled on actual reads by 14 months. Complaint back-bills had a median length of 24 months. Smart meters cut how many meters are left to estimate, but 2-15% of a supplier's smart meters are not sending reads. That share differs by supplier and persists. Access failures fall into several kinds (nobody home, refused, a locked meter cupboard), and only a refusal after documented requests is obstruction.

Theft: in progress at about 1% of domestic electricity meters (Ofgem 2014). Detected at a few per cent of that stock a year. About a quarter of investigations confirm theft: 15% of proactive investigations and 42% of reactive ones. Investigations lean heavily towards prepayment customers and deprived areas. Detected thefts have run for about two years. A supplier's cost of theft through prices is its market share of a national smear, not the theft in its own customer base.

Hard-to-read meters should persist at a property across tenants rather than appearing at random each year, and should be more common among private lets and flats. The size of that tilt is not published. Half-hourly settlement should leave billing for traditional meters unchanged and move the cost of late readings from the individual supplier to the market as a whole after four months.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The duties, entry powers and warrant rules are quoted from the statutes and licence conditions in force. The repeal of the inspection duty is from Ofgem's decision of 4 February 2016. The obstruction test is from Ofgem's 2018 back-billing decision, pages 9-10. The theft safeguards are SLC 12A.11.

THEFT SCALE. RECCo's Theft Estimation Methodology (2023) puts electricity theft at 1,703-2,837 GWh a year and gas theft at 636-1,059 GWh. That is £737m-£1,233m and £93m-£155m at December 2022 cap prices, or £29-48 a household. Ofgem (2025) gives £830m to £1.388bn. The gas industry's UIG expert assumes far more gas theft: 6,362 GWh, or 1.48% of consumption. It says this assumption is 'driven largely by the views of electricity theft' studies. The two gas estimates differ seven- to tenfold.

DETECTION. About 300,000 TRAS investigations ran between 2014 and March 2021, and 23% confirmed theft. For tip-off leads, 37% are investigated and 22% of those confirm theft (Ofgem 2025). Suppliers meet 40% of their incentive-scheme targets. In 2011 suppliers detected 15,956 domestic electricity thefts, against a stock Ofgem put at 275,000 in progress at any time. Reports to the public tip-off line grew from 2,613 in 2017-18 to 13,415 in 2024-25.

READS. Ofgem in 2015 found that meter inspections produced under 4% of suspected gas theft incidents. Tip-offs and suppliers' own analysis produced 85%. Large suppliers' smart meters at the end of 2024 were 85.1% to 98.0% in smart mode.

ADDED 8 OCTOBER 2026. Ofgem's half-hourly settlement decision and business case (20 April 2021), section 3 on the settlement timetable and manual reads. Elexon's announcement of 22 October 2025 on the migration dates. The programme's paper on moving to the new timetable (cut-over planned 2 July 2027, all earlier runs complete by 31 October 2027). English Housing Survey 2022-23, energy annex tables 3.7 and 3.9 (smart meters by tenure and payment method). Ofgem's back-billing decision (5 March 2018, page 8) for the access problems suppliers raised. Alt HAN Co's published figure for home-network range problems.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
No published source gives the share of meter-reading visits that fail. Nor does any give the split of failures into nobody home, refusal and inaccessible meters. This is a question for someone who has run a meter-reading operation, and nothing has been invented to fill it. Also unpublished: how many warrants are sought for theft, safety or reading; the share of long-unread homes a supplier could show were obstructive; the domestic share of the theft estimate; theft rates on smart against traditional meters; and the recovery rate on theft since 2014. The size of electricity GSP group correction across 2016-2025 was not derived. We have not yet checked whether the price cap already allows for UIG and group-correction costs.

On half-hourly settlement: the settlement code's target for actual readings after the cut-over, any reading-frequency rule for traditional meters in the new design, and how the load-shaping service estimates an unread meter were not found. On clustering: no source measures how far no-access persists at a property, or how much more common it is by tenure, landlord, building type or vulnerability. We recommend drawing a persistent hard-to-read group tied to the property rather than the person, sized as now, and spread evenly until a practitioner says how much more often it sits in private lets and flats. That is a recommendation, not an established fact.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a theft rate for any one supplier's customers, and that is deliberate. A supplier pays for theft mostly through a market-wide smear, and it learns about theft among its own customers only through its own investigations. It does not model how a household answers a request for access. The research shows that is what the supplier's reading effort and the obstruction exception both depend on, and the simulation does not yet have it. Changes after 2025 (market-wide half-hourly settlement, the 90-day smart repair rule of 2026) are explained above but fall outside the 2016-2025 window: every settlement day the simulation covers reaches its fourteen-month final run before the planned cut-over.

meta.title: How a GB energy supplier accounts for the bills it will never collect
meta.subtitle: A provision is an estimate made today about money owed today. A write-off comes years later. The cost a supplier reports, and the cost the price cap allows, is the first, not the second.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: the text of IFRS 9, Centrica's annual reports for 2015 to 2025, the 2023-2024 statutory accounts of Octopus Energy, OVO Energy and E.ON Next, and Ofgem's May 2025 decision on debt-related costs. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page. Where nothing published establishes a number, the page says so instead of supplying one.

claim_freshness.source: IFRS 9 (paragraphs 5.4.4, 5.5.15, 5.5.17, B5.5.35, B5.5.37, B5.5.52) as published in Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2067; Centrica plc Annual Reports and Accounts 2016-2025, Note 17 and the Audit and Risk Committee reports; Ofgem, Decision - Appendix 2: Debt-related costs, May 2025; Lowell Group 2013 annual financial results; Arrow Global Group plc Annual Report 2017; Ofgem, Debt Relief Scheme policy update working paper, August 2025; Ofgem, Impact Assessment - Debt Relief Scheme, 6 November 2025
claim_freshness.note: Written because the project carried four different bad-debt figures (three uncited provision tables, a flat 2% of revenue, a per-bill haircut, and the world's write-offs) and none of them was the quantity suppliers and Ofgem report. Working is in docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md. Extended on 8 October 2026 at the director's request to cover what written-off debt sells for and how that and near-zero recovery after write-off enter the provision, a customer's forward value and price (section 9 of the research file).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB supplier's cost of bad debt is the change in its provision plus what it writes off, and at the one supplier that publishes the detail, the provision depends far more on how a customer pays and whether they have left than on how old the debt is: in 2025 Centrica held 7% against direct-debit debt over 90 days old, 50% against pay-on-receipt debt of the same age, and 88% against a closed account's.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Every energy supplier is owed money by some of its customers. At each year-end it has to estimate how much of that money it will never get. That estimate is the provision. It sits on the balance sheet against the money owed.

The yearly cost of bad debt is how much the provision went up, plus anything written off in the year, less anything recovered that had been written off before. It is not the amount written off. A write-off is the step of taking the debt off the books once there is no reasonable hope of collecting it, and it comes late. It does not mean the supplier has stopped chasing: Centrica says enforcement continues on written-off balances.

So three numbers that sound alike are different. The provision is a stock: how much of today's debt is expected to go bad. The bad-debt charge is a flow: what the year cost. A write-off is an event. A model that only books write-offs records the cost years late and misses the cost of customers who stay in debt without leaving.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE RULE. IFRS 9 requires a supplier to hold, against every customer receivable, the loss it expects over the receivable's whole life (paragraph 5.5.15, the simplified approach). The estimate must weigh a range of outcomes, allow for the time value of money, and use reasonable information about the past, the present and forecasts (5.5.17). A supplier may use a provision matrix: rates by how overdue a balance is, in groups whose losses differ (B5.5.35). Historical losses are the anchor but must be adjusted for conditions now and expected (B5.5.52). Default is presumed by 90 days past due unless the supplier can show otherwise (B5.5.37).

HOW A SUPPLIER APPLIES IT. Centrica groups receivables by customer type and by payment method, separates live accounts from closed ones, and ages each customer's whole balance by its oldest unpaid invoice. Rates come from its own history of cash collected, re-estimated each year, plus internal ratings from payment history and credit-bureau data. On top it adds a separate macroeconomic provision when it believes the past understates what is coming: GBP 30m in 2020 and 2021, GBP 125m in 2022, GBP 175m in 2023, GBP 49m in 2024 and GBP 11m in 2025. It treats debt as in default from 60 days past due for some groups up to six to twelve months after a final bill, and writes off only once a period of time has passed since the final bill.

WHY ONE YEAR'S CHARGE IS NOISY. Ofgem, which sets the price cap's debt allowance from suppliers' reported charges, notes that a year's charge mixes provisions for this year's bills with corrections to earlier ones, and that suppliers change their models. One supplier told Ofgem it provided heavily in 2023 and corrected down in 2024.

SELLING DEBT. Debt that a supplier has given up collecting can be sold to a debt purchaser. Lowell paid on average 5.4p per pound of face value for the consumer debt it bought from 2004 to 2013, across all sectors, and began buying from utilities in 2013. Arrow Global paid £223.9m for £2.4bn of face value in 2017, about 9.3p, with 41% of the price for secured loans. Centrica reported money received from selling written-off debt in 2017 but not what it sold. Ofgem, valuing crisis-era energy debt still on suppliers' books for its debt relief scheme, took its worth as about a quarter of face value, the part suppliers had not provided for, and puts the cost of collecting at about 3p per pound.

WHAT THAT MEANS. For the provision: by the time a balance is written off, a supplier should already hold close to all of it, because what comes back afterwards is a few pence in the pound. For a customer's forward value: a likely leaver's closing balance is worth the 10-25p in the pound implied by provision rates on old closed accounts, not its face value, and the sale route adds only a few pence much later. For price: the cap's debt allowance is built from suppliers' bad-debt charges, which already net off recoveries and sale proceeds, so they cannot be priced in twice. On a capped tariff the allowance is the ceiling on bad-debt cost a supplier can recover through price; collecting or selling better improves its margin against the cap, not the cap.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible supplier book, provisioned the way suppliers provision, should show these shapes:
- Coverage rising with age within each group, and the groups ordered direct debit, then pay on receipt, then closed accounts. Centrica 2019-2025: direct debit over 90 days 3-7% (34.8% in 2022, an outlier); pay on receipt over 90 days 38-63%; closed accounts over 90 days 75-90%.
- A closed account under 30 days old provisioned above a live pay-on-receipt account 30-90 days old, in every year.
- Provision coverage of the whole residential book of roughly a third to two fifths (Centrica 34-42%, 2019-2025).
- A bad-debt charge of roughly 1-3% of residential revenue, low in 2021 and high in 2023 (Centrica UK: 1.1% in 2021, 3.1% residential in 2023).
- From 2022, provisions growing much faster than write-offs: Centrica's residential charge was GBP 1,160m over 2022-2025 against GBP 391m written off.
- Recoveries after write-off of a few pence in the pound: Centrica recovered GBP 68m against GBP 1,482m written off over 2017-2025, about 4.6%.
- A cost that responds to the 2022-23 crisis through the provision and an overlay in the year it happens, not years later through write-offs.

- Sale proceeds of a few pence in the pound for written-off consumer debt: 5.4p (all sectors, 2004-2013) to about 9p (a 2017 book including secured loans).

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED.
- The text of IFRS 9 on the simplified approach, the provision matrix, forward-looking adjustment, default and write-off.
- Centrica's UK residential provision by payment method, live or closed, and age band, for seven year-ends, 2019 to 2025, from each year's Note 17.
- Centrica's residential provision movements (charge, write-offs, closing balance), 2015 to 2025, and its recoveries of written-off debt, 2017 to 2025.
- Centrica's bad-debt charge as a share of UK energy supply revenue, 2019 to 2025, its macroeconomic overlay by year, and its provision against debt being recovered through prepayment meters (63-81%, not aged).
- Ofgem's definition of the bad-debt cost it allows in the cap, and its reasons for treating a single year's charge with caution.
- Three more suppliers' statutory accounts for 2023-2024. Octopus, OVO and E.ON Next describe the same method (rates by age, payment method and supply status, from their own collection history), report bad-debt charges of 1.6-3.9% of revenue, and hold provisions of 33-60% of their whole-book receivables. Octopus's 2023 accounts show overdue debt provisioned at 35% under three months old and 92% over twelve.

WHAT IS NOT. Only one supplier publishes its provision by method, age and live or closed status, and Ofgem considered and declined to build an industry table. No supplier publishes the roll rates or cure rates behind its matrix. The time from a final bill to write-off is not published. Coverage beyond 90 days is not split further, except one 2025 auditor's line: GBP 812m of Centrica's GBP 1,038m residential provision related to balances more than 360 days old. No price for selling GB energy debt specifically has been found; the sale prices above are for consumer debt across sectors (Lowell, Arrow Global), and Ofgem's quarter-of-face figure is a valuation of debt still held, not a sale price (Ofgem debt relief scheme working paper, August 2025, and impact assessment, November 2025).

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
Every coverage figure here is one supplier's, and that supplier has an unusually large standard-credit and legacy book. Before 2021 Centrica's residential figures include North America, and 2016-2017 are under the older incurred-loss standard, so the decade is not one series. Whether a balance on a repayment plan keeps its age or moves to its own group, and what a direct-debit balance over 90 days old actually is, are questions for someone who has run a supplier's credit function.

What GB domestic energy debt fetches when sold, by age and for live against closed accounts, is not published; nor is the share of written-off energy debt that is sold rather than kept with a collection agency. Whether energy debt sells above or below other consumer debt is not evidenced either way.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a probability that any household will default. A coverage rate is a ratio of two balances at a year-end, and a charge rate is a ratio of two flows over a year; neither is a default probability. It does not say how long a supplier waits before writing off, or what written-off energy debt in particular sells for; it gives only the all-sector purchase prices and says so. It does not establish how the price cap's GBP 71 allowance splits between bad debt and the cost of chasing it.
